questions.question: How do you create and use a custom exception in Python?
questions.title: Custom Exceptions in Python
questions.direct_answer: Define a class derived from `Exception`, give it a clear `Error` name, raise it for one domain failure, and catch it where recovery is possible.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether a custom type represents a useful domain contract rather than a renamed generic failure.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating many empty types that callers never handle differently, or parsing messages instead of types.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Design the class around a caller decision and include structured fields only when needed.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Custom exceptions give a domain failure a stable, meaningful type.
Inherit from `Exception` or an application-specific subclass.
Use an `Error` suffix and keep the class simple unless structured data is useful.
Raise the custom type where the domain rule is detected.
Catch it at the layer that can recover, translate, or present the failure.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A custom exception is an ordinary Python class used to name a failure that matters to the application. It normally derives from `Exception`, directly or through an application base class, and its name usually ends in `Error`. The benefit is not a different control-flow mechanism; it is a stable type that tells callers what failed without forcing them to inspect message text.

For example, a ticket service can raise `SeatUnavailableError` when the requested seat has already been reserved. A web adapter can catch that type and return a conflict response, while a background worker can catch the same type and record a rejected booking. Both layers understand the domain meaning even if the human-readable message later changes. The error may remain an empty subclass, or it may store useful fields such as `seat_id` and `show_id`.

The class should be raised close to the rule that detects the problem and handled where a complete response is possible. Catching it immediately only to print and continue usually weakens the contract. Built-in exceptions remain better for universal programming contracts: an invalid numeric argument can still be `ValueError`; a business rule such as an unavailable seat deserves its own type.

Custom errors should be focused, serialisable only if needed, and free from unrelated behaviour. They make domain failures explicit, allow precise handling, and keep callers independent of fragile message matching.

sections.title: Design the error around the caller's decision
sections.content:
Start with a question: does a caller need to treat this failure differently from other failures? If yes, a distinct class can become part of the function's public contract. If every caller would handle it exactly like `ValueError`, another class may add noise rather than clarity.

Structured fields are useful when handlers need facts rather than prose. A payment error might carry an order identifier and a retryable flag. Keep a readable message for logs and people, but let code read attributes instead of parsing that message. Calling `super().__init__(message)` ensures the usual exception string and `args` work as expected.

Avoid inheriting from several built-in exception types. Some built-ins have implementation-specific layouts, and Python's documentation recommends one exception base at a time. A small application hierarchy under one `Exception` subclass gives broad and narrow catch points without that risk.

sections.title: Where a domain error belongs
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Domain operation] --> B{Rule satisfied?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Return result]
  B -->|No| D[Raise SeatUnavailableError]
  D --> E[Application boundary]
  E --> F[Map type to an honest response]
```

questions.question: When should an application use a custom exception hierarchy?
questions.title: Custom Exception Hierarchies
questions.direct_answer: Use a small custom hierarchy when callers need one broad application catch point plus specific recovery for a few distinct domain failures.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether exception inheritance is connected to real caller policies.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Building a deep taxonomy with no difference in handling.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the base to show ownership and leaves to enable different decisions.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Create one application base error for failures owned by the application.
Add child types only when callers have different recovery or reporting behaviour.
Catch a child for a precise response and the base for a shared boundary response.
Do not copy Python's entire built-in hierarchy inside one application.
Keep programming bugs outside the domain hierarchy so they remain visible.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A custom exception hierarchy is useful when an application needs both general and specific handling. One base class, such as `CheckoutError`, marks failures that belong to the checkout workflow. Child classes such as `OutOfStockError` and `PaymentDeclinedError` describe cases that may produce different responses. Because matching uses inheritance, a caller can handle one child specially or catch the base class when all checkout failures share the same boundary policy.

For example, an order endpoint may map `OutOfStockError` to a response that suggests changing quantity, while a command-line import may catch any `CheckoutError` and print a concise failure. An unexpected `AttributeError` is not a checkout failure and should not be wrapped automatically, because doing so would disguise a defect as a business outcome.

The hierarchy should stay shallow. A new subclass is justified by a useful decision, not by every sentence the application could display. One inheritance base is normally enough, and messages or fields can carry additional detail. This produces precise recovery without recreating a large taxonomy that no caller uses.

sections.title: Broad handling and narrow recovery can coexist
sections.content:
Think of the base class as ownership: it says which subsystem promises the error. Think of each leaf as behaviour: it exists because some boundary retries, prompts, maps, or reports that case differently.

A handler for the base class can be placed at a job or request boundary to prevent known domain outcomes from becoming unstructured failures. More focused code still catches a child first. Unrelated technical exceptions should either propagate or be explicitly translated with exception chaining, preserving their original cause.

Too many levels make the contract harder to discover. Prefer a base and a small number of meaningful children. Add another level only when several children truly share a policy that callers use.

sections.title: One broad boundary, two specific outcomes
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Exception] --> B[CheckoutError]
  B --> C[OutOfStockError]
  B --> D[PaymentDeclinedError]
  C --> E[Suggest a smaller quantity]
  D --> F[Ask for another payment method]
  B --> G[Shared checkout failure boundary]
```

sections.title: Catch a leaf or the shared base
